data.title: NVDA Stock Sees Biggest Fall In 22 Months, But Top Analyst Says Nvidia’s AI Boom Isn’t Over Yet — Here Are 5 Reasons Why
data.description:
Key points:
  • Nvidia's transition to its Vera Rubin platform appears to be progressing faster than its previous Blackwell ramp, according to Kindig.
  • She argued that investors may be overlooking how product transitions have historically affected Nvidia's growth trajectory.
  • Kindig suggested that the current transition could follow a similar pattern, with temporary growth moderation being mistaken for a longer-term deterioration in demand.

Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) shares saw their worst single-day fall in about 22 months amid concerns of the AI boom running out of steam, with slowing growth expectations, margin pressure and questions over hyperscaler spending weighing on investor sentiment.

IO Fund’s Beth Kindig argued that investors may be mistaking a temporary pause for a fundamental slowdown, pointing to Nvidia's latest results, expanding AI demand and a valuation that has fallen sharply even as growth expectations remain elevated.

Nvidia shares fell more than 14% in Friday’s regular trading, but gained nearly 4% during the afterhours session.

Kindig Says Nvidia's Next-Generation AI Chips Are Already Flexing Muscle

Nvidia's transition to its Vera Rubin platform appears to be progressing faster than its previous Blackwell ramp, according to Kindig. Rubin generated approximately $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, nearly double Blackwell's $11 billion in its initial quarter.

Kindig argued that investors may be overlooking how product transitions have historically affected Nvidia's growth trajectory. During the Blackwell ramp, sequential revenue growth slowed before accelerating again as demand picked up.

She suggested that the current transition could follow a similar pattern, with temporary growth moderation being mistaken for a longer-term deterioration in demand.

Kindig also points to Nvidia's fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook, which implies growth of approximately 75%, up from 70% projected for fiscal 2027 despite a larger revenue base.

AI Demand Is Still Outstripping Supply, Says Kindig

Kindig noted that the defining characteristic of the AI infrastructure boom remains a supply-constrained market in which demand continues to exceed available capacity.

She highlighted that Nvidia's supply-related commitments surged to $390 billion in the third quarter (Q3) of fiscal 2027, up from $119 billion just two quarters earlier. Meanwhile, cloud industry backlog climbed to $2.5 trillion from $2 trillion in just three months.

“Cloud industry backlog now sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, underscoring the significant multi-year opportunity ahead of our partners and of Nvidia,” said Nvidia’s CFO and interim CEO, Collette Kress.

Kindig also pointed to supply constraints elsewhere in the AI ecosystem, including SK Hynix's comments about being effectively sold out through 2029. For her, these figures suggest that the AI infrastructure buildout is far from running out of demand.

Falling AI Costs Could Actually Fuel More Demand

The decline in AI token prices may be creating a counterintuitive effect, wherein cheaper AI services could drive greater usage, ultimately increasing demand for computing infrastructure.

Nvidia reported that token prices have fallen nearly 60% since May, while token consumption has accelerated. Kindig sees this dynamic as an example of “Jevons Paradox,” where improvements in efficiency and lower costs can ultimately lead to greater consumption.

She also highlighted the surprising strength of older GPU generations. Hopper GPUs are reportedly being recontracted at up to twice their original prices under multiyear agreements, while B300 rental rates have risen more than 60% since introduction.

"All of this is creating a powerful flywheel," Kress said.

Kindig argues that AI workloads are increasingly spreading across different GPU generations rather than being concentrated exclusively on the newest hardware, extending the useful economic life of older systems.

She believes that is another sign that AI demand remains robust rather than showing signs of saturation.

What Retail Investors Think Of NVDA Stock

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits around Nvidia trended in the ‘extremely bullish’ territory at the time of writing.

NVDA stock is down 33% year-to-date. The S&P 500 ETF (SPY) is up 4% over the past 12 months, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) is up 4% over the past 12 months.

data.title: Cattle futures rise ahead of bullish USDA feedlot data
data.description:
By Julie Ingwersen

Live cattle futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange rose on Friday for a third straight session as traders squared positions ahead of a monthly government report that analysts expected to show a slight year-on-year decline in the number of cattle in US feedlots.

CME December live cattle settled up 0.150 cent at 223.0 cents per pound, and most-active February futures rose 0.500 cent to 227.700 cents.

January feeder cattle fell 0.125 cent to finish at 335.425 cents per pound.

After the market closed, the US Department of Agriculture reported the number of cattle on feed as of November 1 at 99% of a year ago. Analysts surveyed by Reuters on average had expected a smaller decline, to 99.7%.

The USDA reported cattle placements into US feedlots during October at 93% of a year ago, below the average analyst estimate of 97%. Marketings during October were 95% of a year ago, near the average analyst estimate of 94.9%.

"It was a bullish report all the way around. I would expect futures to be sharply higher on Monday," said Ross Baldwin, broker and market analyst at John Stewart and Associates.

However, steep global declines in equities, led by technology-related shares, raised expectations that consumer demand for beef could slow.

"The big question ... is whether the solid demand we have seen for beef continues, with the huge selloff in the AI shares," said Dan Norcini, an independent livestock trader.

The wholesale choice boxed beef cutout value fell 68 cents to $352.84 per hundredweight on Friday, the USDA said.

CME lean hog futures closed mostly lower, pressured by sagging cash hog prices and weak demand for pork.

December lean hog futures (LHZ26) settled 0.175 cent higher at 52.600 cents per pound while most-active February hogs (LHG27) ended down 1.075 cents at 56.975 cents a pound after setting a contract low at 56.425 cents.

The wholesale pork carcass cutout value fell 78 cents on Friday to $67.88 per cwt, the USDA said, a six-year low.

data.title: Wall Street ends sharply lower on AI selloff, S&P 500, Dow in correction
data.description:
US stocks extended their rout on Friday, and the S&P ​500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic's momentous debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year's stock market rally.

All three major US equity ‌indexes ended sharply lower. The Dow and the S&P 500 are now more than 10% below their record closing highs, confirming both indexes have entered a correction.

The bellwether S&P 500 notched its seventh consecutive drop, its longest losing streak since February 2020.

The S&P 500 and the Dow logged their largest weekly percentage losses since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced his market-rattling "liberation day" tariff package.

The Nasdaq's weekly drop was its largest since March 2020. The tech-heavy index has dipped into negative ​territory for the year.

"This is clearly a challenging day for capital markets, and as we head into a Friday close, appears to be accelerating to a certain ​degree," said Bill Northey, senior investment director at US Bank Wealth Management in Billings, Montana. "But as we step back and evaluate fundamentals and ⁠sentiment, sentiment is clearly winning the day today."

"Sentiment is always the more powerful force in the immediate space, whereas fundamentals tend to win out over time," Northey added, referring to economic ​strength and solid corporate earnings, among other things.

Anthropic's supersized debut as a publicly held company, which was intended to raise as much as $2 trillion in market cap, failed to catch ​fire on Thursday, closing 17.1% above its $83 offer price as enthusiasm for the stock faded throughout the session.

In its second day as a publicly held company, Anthropic's shares fell 9.1%. Nvidia's shares tumbled 13.8%.

The Anthropic IPO, combined with Nvidia's quarterly earnings report, failed to dispel fears over risks associated with artificial intelligence and the massive expenditures on the nascent technology.

"Nvidia reported what might have been one of the greatest quarters in corporate ​earnings history; they did everything right," said Chuck Carlson, chief executive officer at Horizon Investment Services in Hammond, Indiana. "A lot of people, myself included, were looking to the Anthropic debut to ​some extent as a clearing event, and it wasn't."

The Philadelphia SE Semiconductor Index <.SOX>, which has powered much of the broader stock market's gains in recent months, was up as much as 106.6% in ‌mid-June. That ⁠luster has faded, with the index's year-to-date advance having shrunk to 18.7%.

Among hyperscalers, Amazon fell 3.9%, while Meta dropped 5.9%.

Neocloud firm CoreWeave fell 12.1% and its peer Nebius slid 16.1%.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33, the S&P 500 lost 265.41 points, or 3.70%, to 6,910.42 and the Nasdaq Composite lost 1,261.47 points, or 5.28%, to 22,617.73.

The CBOE Market Volatility Index <.VIX>, often referred to as Wall Street's "fear gauge," rose to its highest close since April 7, 2025.

INFLATION, FED IN FOCUS

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said the central bank's ​policy rate is not high enough to ​deal with inflation levels.

Markets are pricing a near-certain ⁠likelihood of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.

Next week's personal consumption expendituresfigures will provide further clarity on the Fed's monetary policy path after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last week.

Among other movers, Intuit shares ​fell 12.8% after the company cut its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, five years ​after acquiring it for ⁠nearly three times as much.

UnitedHealth (UNH.N), opens new tab rose 2.8% after TD Cowen upgraded its shares to a "buy" from a "hold" rating.

The AI selloff also sent Caterpillar 5% lower on worries over weakening demand for its power-generating and backup power equipment.

Cryptocurrency firms including Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood tumbled between 6.3% and 9.6% after bitcoin dropped below the $60,000 level.

Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 3.77-to-1 ratio on the NYSE. There were 38 ⁠new highs ​and 1,199 new lows on the NYSE.

On the Nasdaq, 928 stocks rose and 3,964 fell as declining issues ​outnumbered advancers by a 4.27-to-1 ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 3 new 52-week highs and 28 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 21 new highs and 826 new lows.

Volume on US exchanges was 25.19 billion shares, compared with ​the 19.50 billion average for the full session over the last 20 trading days.

data.title: US Market Crash: Nasdaq enters 'bear market' - 10 things for investors to know
data.description:
US markets had a brutal day on Friday amidst intense selling pressure as the AI trade continued to unwind. The Dow Jones fell another 950 points, taking the drop for the week to 4,100 points. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% on Friday, while the Nasdaq indices - Composite and 100, fell over 5.5% each.

The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6% on Friday, capping its worst week since March 2020. At its intraday low, the index had slumped more than 20% from its recent record high, meaning it had momentarily slumped into a "bear market". For the Dow, it was also the worst week since March 2020 with a 8% drop, while the S&P 500 had its worst weekly performance since April 2025.

With Friday's fall, both the Dow Jones and the S&P 500 have entered a "technical correction", meaning a 10% or more fall from the peak. The Nasdaq, has reversed all the gains for the year, and has now turned negative on a year-to-date basis.

Chipmaker and software stocks continued to remain the worst hit on Friday. Nvidia shares fell 14% on Friday. AMD, which fell 8% on Thursday after the short-seller report, fell another 13% the next day. Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius Group fell 12% and 16% respectively, while Micron, Sandisk and Western Digital, the high-flyers of the year on the S&P 500, fell between 12% and 16% on Friday.

Nvidia's troubles just don't seem to end. The stock fell 22% this week, the seventh straight weekly loss reported by the company. The last instance the stock fell for seven straight weeks? During the global financial crisis of 2008. Reuters reported that the US Securities & Exchanges Commission is exploring possible accounting issues at the company.

Anthropic, the biggest IPO of the world on record, had a dream debut on Thursday, listing at a 34% premium to its issue price of $83. However, the sell-off trimmed those gains to 17% on listing day, and knocked off another 8.5% on Friday, taking the stock back to nearly the same as its issue price, closing at $88.91.

Gold prices also continued to slide for the fifth day running, marking their biggest weekly fall since March this year. Fears of the US Federal Reserve aggressively hiking rates to combat inflation, along with a rout in AI stocks, is causing this widespread sell-off, not just in gold, but in other precious and industrial metals as well. Gold is now down 9% for the week, fell to its lowest levels since September 2025, and is decisively below the $4,000 an ounce mark, which many investors felt could be a floor for the fall. Silver is down 15% for the week.

The sell-off in AI stocks has spurred demand for haven assets. The US 10-year yield fell below the 5% mark again on Friday, sliding to 4.95%, while the Yen and the Swiss Franc strengthened against the US Dollar. The Yen gained 0.7% against the greenback, while the Franc snapped an eight-day losing streak. That has prevented the US Dollar index from breaking past the mark of 104, which it currently finds itself near.

While the high-beta names sold-off sharply overnight, investors chose to find some shelter in traditional, old-economy defensive names. Shares of Walmart, Costco, Johnson & Johnson, and Procter & Gamble saw shares gain between 1% to 1.5% overnight, but that could not prevent the 30-stock Dow Jones from falling another 950 points on Friday.

Is the sell-off done? A top technical analyst in the US said NO. Jonathan Krinsky, appearing on CNBC on Friday said that the technical setup doesn't point to the fact that the sell-off is over. He cited Apple, currently the most valuable company in the world, which is only down 3% to 4% from its highs, stating that whenever the S&P 500 has dropped 8% or more from its peak, by the time it makes its final bottom, the average drawdown in Apple has been 23%! He also added that more than 50% of S&P 500 stocks are still above their 50-Day Moving Average, compared to a number below 40% or even 20% when the S&P 500 forms a durable bottom.

data.title: The Blame Game Has Begun Over Anthropic's Turbulent Trading Debut — WSJ
data.description:
By Corrie Driebusch, Kate Clark, Peter Rudegeair and Ben Dummett

Anthropic and its advisers knew they were taking a risk staging its initial public offering during the most intense turbulence in the artificial-intelligence trade to date. They didn't anticipate running into the perfect storm.

Now, Wall Street is sorting through why the biggest-ever IPO stumbled on its second day of trading, as Anthropic shed some $109 billion from its market value. A blame game has begun among investors and others who cite everything from angry fund managers shut out of the offering to poor planning by banks to explain the damage.

Shares of Anthropic dropped as much as 15% Friday — a mere 5 cents above its IPO price — before recovering some ground to close down 8.5% at $88.91. It remains 7% above its IPO price.

The slide from its first-day pop punctuates a period of turmoil for the AI trade. After weeks of growing anxiety among investors over everything from rising borrowing costs for cloud-computing firms to the ramifications of the sex-and-spy scandal at Nvidia, there was optimism that Anthropic could come to the rescue. Maybe AI's pure-play juggernaut would press the big reset button. That didn't happen.

Many other pillars of the AI trade fell along with Anthropic on Friday, from Nvidia to Meta to Oracle, sealing a $4 trillion wipeout for the pillars over the week. The carnage endangers the ambitions of Anthropic's chief rival, OpenAI, which is eager to make its own public market debut next year and is in the process of another mega fundraising round that values the company at $1.25 trillion.

People close to Anthropic and its lead underwriters maintain the IPO is a success, emphasizing they raised more than $100 billion in the IPO and concurrent share sale, and that the stock remains above its IPO price despite one of the worst market selloffs in history.

Still, the tide began turning for Anthropic almost immediately. Its shares opened for trading Thursday a little before noon more than 30% above the IPO price. But the exuberance dissipated quickly, and they spent much of the day losing steam, closing up 17%.

Some investors question how the company and its bankers doled out the $81 billion worth of shares in the IPO. More than half went to investors who already had stakes in the company, including Altimeter Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures, according to people familiar with the matter, an unusually high portion reflecting Anthropic executives' desire to reward early backers.

Some of those early backers were venture-capital firms, which were prevented from selling their pre-existing stakes. Those firms don't typically get big allotments in IPO shares, which they would be free to sell immediately to lock in gains.

Anthropic also allocated significant portions of IPO shares to big investment firms such as Citadel, leading some who were shut out to speculate that the company gave priority to large users of its Claude model, people familiar with the matter said.

Companies and their advisers typically pore over investor requests and spend days curating the optimal shareholder registry to ensure the stock performs well and has a stable ownership base.

Some people familiar with the matter estimated that around 60% of firms that asked to buy shares at the IPO price, many of them hedge funds and large mutual funds, got nothing.

Many other investors received only a portion of what they asked for, with investing giant BlackRock getting about half of the roughly $10 billion allocation it requested, The Wall Street Journal has reported.

Some on Wall Street raised other potential issues, with one hedge-fund manager wondering if the bankers who help decide when and at what level to open shares for trading overshot the opening price, creating an opportunity for downward momentum that can be hard to reverse. The risk of waiting to open shares is that the price could have continued to rise.

Anthropic's IPO also had a unique provision that allowed some current and former employees to immediately sell around 300 million shares, or around $26 billion worth at the IPO price. Typically, employees are subject to lockups that prevent them from selling for several months. Sales of those shares likely added downward pressure on the company's stock.

In San Francisco, several AI employees said they largely disregarded the selloff in Anthropic stock. Instead, they were preoccupied by an Anthropic mathematician's claim on Friday that Claude had solved a Millennium Prize Problem that has stumped humans for 167 years.

Many took the claim as a sign that AI was outpacing human intelligence. Besides, even at its lower stock price, many Anthropic employees' shares are still worth millions of dollars more than they were at the start of this week, the employees said.

From the perspective of bankers on the offering, it remains a success — as long as the company's shares don't fall below the IPO price.

Should that happen, one of the tools bankers could use to stabilize shares will be unavailable. The company announced Friday morning that Anthropic's so-called green-shoe option had already been exercised.

The green shoe effectively allows underwriters to distribute 15% more shares of the deal size to investors in the IPO. The underwriters can then buy those shares back from the company at the IPO price, or, if the stock falls below the IPO price, buy them back in the open market to buoy the stock.

On Dec. 15, another roughly 300 million shares of Anthropic will become available to trade, which could pressure the stock even more.

Write to Corrie Driebusch at corrie.driebusch@wsj.com, Kate Clark at kate.clark@wsj.com, Peter Rudegeair at peter.rudegeair@wsj.com and Ben Dummett at ben.dummett@wsj.com

data.title: Binance hack: $2.82 billion frozen, only $32 million recovered
data.description:
Three weeks after the $6.4 billion Binance hack, investigators report that authorities have frozen $2.82 billion of the stolen assets. The amount actually recovered so far is $32 million.

That gap is the story. Freezing money stops thieves from spending it. Recovering money puts it back where it belongs, and that second step is moving at a crawl.

The breach hit Binance on October 29, 2026. Attackers drained an estimated $6.3 to $6.4 billion in digital assets from the exchange's hot wallets, which are the internet-connected wallets exchanges use to process day-to-day withdrawals.

The whole thing reportedly took 20 to 30 minutes.

The attack has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean state-linked hacking group. The same group has been tied to a previous incident at Bybit, another crypto exchange.

The freeze figures look impressive at first glance. Government and private-sector partners have frozen or intercepted roughly $2.7 to $2.85 billion of the stolen assets, with investigators putting the figure at $2.82 billion.

Roughly $2.3 billion of the frozen funds sits in USDT and USDC. Those are stablecoins, tokens pegged to the US dollar, and their issuers can lock specific balances on-chain.

The US Department of Justice secured court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion of the stolen funds.

In mid-November, Binance obtained a worldwide freezing injunction from the Abu Dhabi Global Market courts to support its recovery efforts. A worldwide freezing order is designed to stop assets from being moved or disposed of across jurisdictions while legal proceedings play out.

Yet public reports point to limited success in getting funds back to Binance or its customers beyond those freezes.

Binance did not wait for the recovery process. The exchange pledged to cover all affected customer balances and set aside more than $6.34 billion from company reserves to do it.

That coverage was completed by November 12, 2026, about two weeks after the attack.

Customers still headed for the exits. After Binance resumed withdrawals, it saw net customer outflows of about $4.7 billion.

For Binance, the math is uncomfortable. The exchange has fronted more than $6.34 billion to cover customers, while recovered funds stand at $32 million. Every dollar that stays frozen rather than returned is effectively a dollar the company has absorbed for now.

The frozen $2.82 billion represents potential upside if courts eventually release it. Legal proceedings across multiple jurisdictions, including US seizure actions and the Abu Dhabi injunction, tend to move on court calendars rather than blockchain timelines.

For the wider industry, the episode highlights two realities at once. Stablecoin issuers proved they can act quickly to freeze stolen funds. At the same time, the bulk of what was taken did not land in freezable form.

The hack has also put exchange security practices under scrutiny, particularly around hot wallets. A loss of this size inside a half-hour window raises obvious questions about how much value exchanges keep in internet-connected wallets and how quickly unusual withdrawals can be halted.

What to watch next: whether the DOJ's authorization over more than $1.2 billion converts into actual returned funds, how the Abu Dhabi injunction is enforced across borders, and whether the frozen stablecoin balances get released to Binance. Until those pieces move, the recovery scoreboard reads $32 million against a theft measured in billions.

data.title: The Brother-Sister Duo Who Want to Keep Anthropic Weird — WSJ
data.description:
By Berber Jin, Maxwell Zeff and Keach Hagey

Two years before she pulled off the largest public offering of all time, Daniela Amodei gathered everyone at Anthropic in a 16-acre garden on a sweltering fall day near the Santa Cruz mountains.

The AI company now with a market value of roughly $1.18 trillion was at the time still a young startup that Amodei and her big brother, Dario, had co-founded with five friends. It was undergoing a hiring spree and Daniela was worried. So they carted 10-foot-tall bookshelves onto the grass to make reading nooks, played games and made friendship bracelets. As the company's president, and keeper of its culture, the younger Amodei wanted to deliver a message.

"Keep Anthropic weird," Daniela told them.

Anthropic embraces being atypical because it believes the artificial intelligence future will be anything but normal. Many co-founders meet in college, or at a first job. This pair met when he was 4 and she was born.

Thursday morning, they hugged to ring the opening bell in an IPO initially celebrated as a triumph and then just as dizzyingly devolved into a blame game on Wall Street Friday as the shares spun down. Shares would rise 30% in its first hours before dropping Friday close to their offering price. In a sign of just how huge it all was, even after the fall, each sibling ended Friday with a stake over $21 billion.

Dario Amodei, 43, the company's chief executive, is Anthropic's ideological leader. He hosts regular all-staff meetings called "Dario Vision Quests," to share his unfiltered thoughts on AI progress, politics and the tech industry. He once attended a developer meeting with a loaf of bread on his head because why not. He only has one direct report, his chief of staff.

Daniela, 39, the company's president and board chair, oversees day-to-day operations and manages the executive team. She collects stuffed animals. She loves pigs. And her husband, Holden Karnofsky, joined the company last year.

"Dario makes us ambitious, I make us successful," Daniela said in a podcast interview with biographer Walter Isaacson recorded in July. It would be "complicated" to execute the company's strategy without her, she said. Without Dario, "Anthropic could be a good, successful business — but not change the world."

That's meant some unusual choices. Anthropic has since its founding warned about extreme risks of AI development — and also accelerated in a race to develop the most powerful AI models. It screens out new hires who care more about money than its safety-focused mission with what it calls "culture interviews" about its values. And it's researching whether its core products might be conscious — something that has drawn rebukes, and some outright scorn, from rivals.

In the prospectus for Thursday's offering, Anthropic warned that "sufficiently advanced AI systems," without security measures, could "pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

Dario and Daniela grew up in San Francisco's Mission district, less than 3 miles from what would become Anthropic's headquarters. They say they developed a uniquely close relationship. Dario taught Daniela how to play videogames as a child and how to drive as a teenager.

Their mother, Elena Engel, worked as a project manager overseeing the construction and renovation of public libraries across the San Francisco Bay. Their father, Riccardo Amodei, was a leather-goods designer from a small town in Tuscany, Italy.

The Amodei parents separated in 1991, when Dario was 8 and his sister was 3, according to city court records viewed by the Journal. Their parents filed for divorce 14 years later, in 2005.

Dario went to college at the California Institute of Technology, where he was accepted into Physics 11, a freshman course that selected students based on their solutions to a pair of difficult research problems known as "hurdles."

As a sophomore at Caltech, Dario protested the Iraq war. "We who create the technology that fuels this nation are profoundly distressed that it be used indiscriminately for war," Dario told the Pasadena City Council in March 2003, reading a student petition.

If Dario was a budding scientist, transferring to Stanford and then pursuing a Ph.D. at Princeton University studying physics then biology, Daniela embraced the humanities. The younger Amodei attended University of California, Santa Cruz, on a classical flute scholarship, and graduated with a degree in literature.

Their father, Riccardo, died in 2006 of hepatitis C, a disease that became largely curable just a few years later. Dario would later cite his loss as a reason to develop AI that could accelerate medical discoveries.

Shortly after his father's death, Dario stumbled upon GiveWell, a charity evaluator founded by two former Bridgewater Associates analysts, Elie Hassenfeld and Karnofsky, Daniela's future husband, who blogged about their decisions. GiveWell and other blogs introduced Dario to the fundamental ideas of effective altruism, a social movement that uses reasoning and rationality to maximize a person's positive impact.

On visits home from Princeton, Dario talked late into the night with Daniela about making the world better, which included sharing ideas from GiveWell, the two recounted on a podcast in 2022. When they founded Anthropic, each pledged 80% of their founding equity to charity. As of Friday, that would come to over $17 billion per sibling.

After graduating from college, Daniela worked on international development in Washington, D.C., which eventually led her to a five-month fellowship in Uganda.

Dario began considering a career in tech. He met Elon Musk in 2010 through an introduction from Tom Tombrello, the Caltech professor who created Physics 11, and visited SpaceX offices. Dario was offered a job by Musk, but he declined, believing his skills were better suited to computational biology than propulsion engineering.

Dario returned to Stanford as a postdoc. There, he co-founded the Vannevar Group, a forum to discuss ways to accelerate scientific progress. Among its early members was Jared Kaplan, now Anthropic's chief scientist. Attendance wasn't always perfect.

"This week lots of people are at Burning Man, so we won't have a meeting today," Dario wrote in an email in August 2013, referring to the yearly Nevada counterculture festival.

The next year he attended Burning Man, too, at the prodding of his new girlfriend, Cami Clark, and other friends, recalled Naureen Nayyar, who also went.

Dario visited the group house in the Presidio where Nayyar lived. She recalls Amodei saying that he would need to go into business if he wanted to do the most good. "He made a very intentional decision to shift away from academia," Nayyar said.

In 2013, Daniela returned to San Francisco for a job at Stripe and moved into a group house near the city's Glen Park neighborhood with her brother and Karnofsky, who had become Dario's friend.

The group home — which housed more than half of Anthropic's founding team over the years — became a place where the Amodeis, Karnofsky and effective altruist friends could explore ideas both serious and whimsical.

One was Power Smoothie, a blueberry-kale beverage Karnofsky designed based on a formula from Dario to maximize nutrition and convenience, while minimizing animal suffering. "Overall I'd be surprised if anyone could consume enough Power Smoothie in their lifetime to account for two cows," Karnofsky wrote on a website about the drink.

Daniela and Karnofsky started dating, and moved into a room above the house's garage. By 2016, Karnofsky proposed to Daniela with a feature-length film starring the roughly "50 stuffed animals we have in our room," according to a blog post he wrote about the proposal. The film's plot was partially based on a favorite TV show of Daniela's, he said, "Buffy The Vampire Slayer."

The invitation to their wedding the following year stated that they were excited about effective altruism and asked guests to make donations in lieu of gifts. In the summer of 2023, Daniela joined GiveWell's board of directors, and remains there to this day. Karnofsky served as the vice chair of GiveWell's board until August 2023, according to government filings.

After effective altruism's most famous proponent, Sam Bankman-Fried, went to prison, many tied to the movement distanced themselves from it. In interviews with media outlets, Dario has said he doesn't consider himself to be an effective altruist, and Daniela has said she doesn't identify with the term.

Daniela still lives in the former group house, which she now shares with Karnofsky and their two children. Dario is married to Cami Clark. The couple doesn't have children.

While working at Stripe, Daniela got to know the company's then chief technology officer, Greg Brockman, who would occasionally visit the Amodei group house. In 2015, when founding OpenAI, Brockman tried unsuccessfully to recruit Dario to join; Dario came aboard in 2016. There, he engaged in debates with his fellow employees, suggesting that immersive videogames might be a solution for the political strife caused by AI-induced joblessness, according to widely circulated Slack messages.

Roughly a year after Daniela's 2017 wedding, which Brockman attended, he recruited Daniela to work at OpenAI, too, uniting the Amodei siblings at one company for the first time.

It wasn't long before the Amodeis and Brockman started to clash over turf and safety. Dario and some other like-minded staffers — who came to be known as "the pandas," after Dario's favorite animal — defected. In 2020 they left, and the next year formed a competing AI lab — Anthropic.

data.title: US House unconstitutionally passed spending bill in 2022, court rules
data.description:
By Nate Raymond

The US House of Representatives unconstitutionally passed a $1.7 trillion government funding bill in 2022 through a pandemic-era rule allowing lawmakers to vote by proxy rather than in person, a federal appeals court ruled on Friday.

The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals voted 9-8 to uphold an injunction that outgoing Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secured blocking enforcement of a provision of that measure that gave pregnant workers stronger legal protections.

Democrat Nancy Pelosi, the speaker of the House at the time, helped implement the proxy voting rule in May 2020 following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic as an emergency measure. The rule was ditched when Republicans took control of the House after the November 2022 elections.

Before Republicans took control, the House used the proxy voting rule to pass a spending package that included the provision Paxton challenged, called the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act. It was signed into law by Democratic President Joe Biden.

The bill passed the House on a 225-201 vote, with 226 members voting by proxy.

Friday's ruling, powered by the 5th Circuit's conservative majority, held that the proxy rule violated the US Constitution's quorum clause, which the court said requires a majority of House members to be physically present to pass legislation.

"While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause’s constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat," wrote US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, an appointee of Republican President Donald Trump.

While the decision concerns how the entire bill was passed, the relief that the 5th Circuit granted Paxton's office was narrow, as it barred the US Department of Justice and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from enforcing the pregnant workers provision against Texas.

The DOJ, which defended the law, and Paxton's office did not respond to requests for comment.

US Circuit Judge James Graves, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama, in a dissenting opinion called the ruling "illogical, inexplicable, and invalid."

He said the majority read a physical-presence requirement into the quorum clause that does not exist. Graves said the majority provided no explanation for why, if the entirety of the law was unconstitutionally passed, its ruling "should be limited only to one small sliver of the multitrillion dollar bill."

data.description:
HONG KONG, Nov 20, 2026 - (ACN Newswire) - 16 November, The No. 4 graphitization furnace unit of the 200,000 tonnes-per-annum integrated lithium battery anode material project of Xiangfu New Energy was successfully energized and commenced operation, marking a major milestone in project development and a further expansion of production capacity.

Xiangfu New Energy is an indirect non-wholly-owned subsidiary of China Risun Group Limited ("China Risun" or the "Group"). Previously, Risun Group Limited, a wholly-owned subsidiary of China Risun, proposed to make a capital injection of RMB506.94 million in cash into Xiangfu New Energy. Upon completion of the transaction, Tianjin Binhai Energy & Development Co., Ltd. ("Binhai Energy"), an indirect non-wholly-owned subsidiary of the Group, and Risun Group Limited will hold approximately 51.5% and 18.64% equity interests in Xiangfu New Energy, respectively. On November 19, 2026, the Group convened an extraordinary general meeting to approve and confirm the Capital Injection Agreement and the supplemental agreement in relation to the connected transaction, with all three ordinary resolutions set out in the circular duly passed by way of poll.

As the Group's core operating platform for lithium battery anode materials under Binhai Energy, Xiangfu New Energy focuses on the production, research and development of lithium battery anode materials across the entire industrial value chain, supported by integrated green power projects featuring source-grid-load-storage systems. The Company principally engages in the production of artificial graphite anode materials, with operations covering the complete production process, including upstream raw material processing, graphitization heat treatment and downstream coating of finished products. Its products are widely used in power batteries, energy storage batteries and consumer batteries.

Since the commencement of construction, work on the graphitization furnace units has been subject to a demanding schedule and a complex, multi-stage construction process, encompassing civil engineering works, furnace lining construction, electrical system installation, equipment installation and commissioning. Faced with challenges including stringent equipment installation precision requirements and extensive cross-disciplinary coordination, various departments of the Company worked closely with construction contractors to advance the project. Construction personnel remained committed on-site, closely monitoring every detail of the works and systematically overcoming commissioning challenges. Through around-the-clock efforts to accelerate progress while maintaining strict standards for construction quality and workplace safety, the Company successfully ensured the timely energization and commissioning of the No. 4 furnace unit.

Graphitization is a core process in the production of anode materials, and the commissioning and operation of graphitization furnace units directly determine the release of finished anode material production capacity. The successful energization and commencement of operation of the No. 4 furnace unit represents an important milestone in the project development process. It effectively expands the Company's graphitization capacity, enhances its overall production and supply capabilities, and plays a significant role in stabilizing product output and ensuring reliable fulfilment of customer orders.

Building on this achievement, the Company will continue to ensure the stable operation of commissioned furnace units while strengthening production management, operational maintenance, process optimisation and safety control to steadily unlock existing capacity. At the same time, it will accelerate the construction of the remaining project facilities, coordinate equipment commissioning, personnel deployment and process refinement, and facilitate the phased commissioning of additional production units.

Looking ahead, Xiangfu New Energy will remain focused on its strategic development objectives by continuously improving its end-to-end production system, expanding industrial scale, refining anode material manufacturing technologies, and attracting and cultivating professional technical and production talent. The Company will continue advancing towards its goal of becoming an innovative and industry-leading new energy enterprise.

SAN DIEGO, Nov. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Capricor Therapeutics , a biotechnology company developing transformative cell and exosome-based therapeutics for rare diseases, today announced that it received a Complete Response Letter (CRL) from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its resubmitted Biologics License Application (BLA) for Deramiocel, its investigational cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD). The CRL states that the FDA does not consider the data sufficient to establish substantial evidence of effectiveness and cites certain other clinical deficiencies.

“We are deeply disappointed for the boys and young men living with Duchenne and their families,” said Linda Marbán, Ph.D., Capricor’s Chief Executive Officer. “Deramiocel has been studied in two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, HOPE-2 and HOPE-3, both of which met their primary endpoints. We stand behind the rigor of our clinical program and the integrity of our data, and we believe the data support approval. We are reviewing the letter carefully and will share next steps once we have completed our evaluation.”

As of September 30, 2026, the Company had cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and marketable securities of approximately $198.5 million, which it believes is sufficient to fund its planned operations for at least the next 12 months. About Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a severe, X-linked genetic disorder characterized by progressive muscle degeneration affecting the skeletal, respiratory, and cardiac muscles. It is caused by the absence of functional dystrophin, a key structural protein in muscle cells. DMD affects approximately 15,000 individuals in the United States, primarily males. Over time, deterioration of the heart muscle leads to cardiomyopathy and heart failure, the leading cause of death in DMD. There is no cure, and treatment options remain limited.

Deramiocel (CAP-1002) consists of allogeneic cardiosphere-derived cells (CDCs), a rare population of cardiac cells that have been shown in preclinical and clinical studies to exert immunomodulatory and anti-fibrotic actions in the preservation of skeletal and cardiac muscle function in muscular dystrophies such as DMD. CDCs act by secreting extracellular vesicles known as exosomes, which target macrophages and alter their expression profile to adopt a healing rather than pro-inflammatory phenotype. For the treatment of DMD, Deramiocel holds Orphan Drug, RMAT and Rare Pediatric Disease designations in the U.S., and Orphan Drug and ATMP designations in Europe.

Capricor Therapeutics is a biotechnology company dedicated to advancing cell and exosome-based therapeutics for the treatment of rare diseases. data.title: Oxford and MIT Didn't Bite. So Ken Griffin Took His Miami Campus Elsewhere. — WSJ
data.description:
By Deborah Acosta, Douglas Belkin, Jenny Strasburg and Juliet Chung

Ken Griffin has been talking to elite universities about his vision to remake the city of Miami for the last several years. He wanted to turn his new home into a global business hub, and to make that happen, South Florida needed a top technology school.

The universities of Oxford and Cambridge, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Vanderbilt University were among the institutions with which he held discussions.

In September, the Citadel chief executive announced that he would invest $2 billion in a partnership with Carnegie Mellon University to build a brand-new Miami campus. Another $1 billion would go to CMU's main campus in Pittsburgh.

A CMU press release referred to the combined $3 billion investment as the largest individual gift in higher education history.

The gift was striking not just for its size: Griffin is not an alumnus of the school. He has donated to other academic institutions, including at least half a billion dollars to his alma mater Harvard, but this project has ambition to help reshape a city.

"We regularly engage with leading universities, but the vision and model we developed with Carnegie Mellon over two years was unique," said a Citadel spokesman in a statement, citing the school's strength in computing and robotics among other attributes.

The scale of the investment reflects the big changes sweeping through higher education.

Elite academic institutions are weighing distant satellite campuses and unconventional partnerships as they grapple with shrinking student demographics, slower tuition growth, and the soaring costs of expanding AI and technology programs.

It also reflects significant changes in Miami.

In a few short years, thanks in part to a low-tax, pro-business environment, the city has become a magnet for some of the most powerful people in America, who are putting down roots in hopes that Miami could one day go toe-to-toe with Wall Street and Silicon Valley.

Griffin has had an outsize role in this transformation. He announced in 2022 that he would move the headquarters of Citadel, the hedge-fund firm he founded, and his market-making firm Citadel Securities, to Miami from Chicago. His plans include a 52-story Citadel headquarters as well as other major office and residential real estate acquisitions.

Griffin meets regularly with leaders of top schools about topics including expanding access to higher education and has made significant donations to several. His discussions with the universities about a Miami campus were wide ranging and the level of detail varied.

Griffin approached leadership at MIT with his vision for a Miami campus within the past four years, people familiar with the matter said. While the university has helped Singapore and Russia establish their own universities — Singapore University of Technology and Design and the Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology in Moscow — it generally avoids creating satellite campuses, which are viewed by some administrators as logistical and administrative headaches. Nothing came of the talks.

Griffin also had discussions in 2024 with top administrators at the University of Oxford in the U.K. to discuss the possibility of an Oxford campus in Miami that would include his financial support, according to people familiar with the talks. Some Oxford officials expressed enthusiasm about pursuing a potential agreement with Griffin but ran into opposition from other officials, the people say.

Griffin also had some preliminary conversations with Cambridge about a new university, but they stopped short of formal proposals, a person familiar with the conversations said.

Officials at Vanderbilt University met with Griffin as that university explored plans for an expansion that has led to Vanderbilt outposts in four cities including New York and San Francisco.

Instead of Miami, Vanderbilt ultimately went to West Palm Beach. An alumnus, Cody Crowell, had recognized the opportunity for Vanderbilt and brought it up with Chancellor Daniel Diermeier at a football game in 2023.

The school worked with real-estate moguls Stephen Ross and Jeff Greene to acquire land in West Palm Beach for a Florida campus.

Griffin's conversations with CMU started about two years ago.

The new campus will be built on 35-acres in Miami's Wynwood neighborhood. About $1.1 billion was used to buy part of the site, which was owned by local real-estate developer Moishe Mana. Mana also helped Griffin's team acquire additional properties in the neighborhood for the campus.

Some $900 million will go toward building a campus. According to the announcement of the partnership, development plans include space for industry research labs and venture studios so students, faculty, industry and community partners can work alongside one another. The school will support more than 3,500 undergraduate, master's and Ph.D. students, nearly 300 faculty and over 600 staff members.

Construction is slated to begin in 2027, with the first students expected to enroll in 2028.

Griffin's multiyear effort underscores how complicated big donations can be for schools.

Even as universities are under greater financial stress than ever, the sector is consolidating and many research universities are eager to expand. Presidents routinely spend half of their time soliciting major donations, often to support expansion goals.

But there are risks to these kinds of gifts: They can take years to land and come with expectations, implicit or laid out in the black-and-white of a gift agreement. Poorly aligned interests can cause indigestion to institutions that prioritize their academic and operational autonomy.

University presidents are often hired for their fundraising prowess and judged on the projects they build. Trustees often have relationships with donors and are also eager to land big gifts. Turning down one prospective donor risks turning off the next donor who may be considering a gift of their own.

And even billionaire-funded projects that are unrestricted can generate unforeseen expenses and cost overruns.

"Development officers have a phrase for these potential donations: gifts that eat," said Ben Porter, founder of Principal Gift Strategies, a fundraising consulting firm.

For CMU President Farnam Jahanian, a Miami outpost offers a strategic expansion into a growing tech ecosystem at the ground floor, and a base from which to recruit elite Latin American engineering talent.

CMU is ranked highly in disciplines Griffin is interested in — computer science, artificial intelligence, robotics and quantitative finance — and for decades Citadel has tapped CMU as a prime recruiting pipeline for software engineers and quantitative analysts. In 2015 the university named a computer science lab and study space the Citadel Teaching Commons after Citadel donated money and equipment.

Though the CMU board of trustees voted unanimously to open the satellite campus in Miami, it took a prolonged negotiation by Griffin to get to an agreement with the school.

Griffin joined the board of trustees as part of the investment, and Paul Darrah, Citadel's chief workplace officer, is currently helping to manage the development project. CMU said it would soon be hiring a development officer and that the school would be "responsible for building the campus, setting the academic standards, recruiting faculty and advancing the educational and research mission of CMU Miami."

It could not be learned how the land ownership will be structured. To secure the 30-plus acres in Miami, Griffin tapped Citadel executives — including Gerald Beeson, Citadel's COO, and Cason Carter, Citadel's head of public affairs — to work with local partners to present Mana with a deal.

By the end of October, Gov. Ron DeSantis nominated the area in and around the campus as an Opportunity Zone, a federal tax designation that allows investors to defer and sometimes avoid taxes when they plow capital gains into real estate and other businesses located within it.

A few weeks earlier, on Oct. 1, DeSantis was in attendance at the announcement party in Miami for the CMU campus, as were local mayors, Citadel executives, and CMU administrators and trustees.

The invitation-only crowd mingled in a Wynwood warehouse decorated by lush potted palms. One CMU trustee expressed anxiety about a possible uphill battle for the school as it works to raise the rest of the funds it will need to make the campus successful.

Griffin walked into the party out of a torrential downpour, stepping out from under an umbrella as he put on his suit jacket. "It's like rain on your wedding day," he quipped.

data.title: Activist Nelson Peltz Walked Away From the Investment He Loved Most. Now He's Back. — WSJ
data.description:
By Heather Haddon

The two men battling for Wendy's have known each other for years, both hold the brand dear and couldn't be more different.

On one side is Nelson Peltz, a brash Brooklynite known for his decades of corporate activism, proxy fights and lengthy white papers criticizing management. Peltz cut his activist teeth with Wendy's more than two decades ago, and has been fixated with the brand since.

In the company's corner is Bob Wright, a mild-mannered, Midwestern CEO who once worked with the chain's founder Dave Thomas. Returning to Wendy's for a third time in May, he brought boxes of brand memorabilia to outfit his office and counts among his contacts the original Wendy, daughter of the founder who still owns restaurants in the chain.

Peltz acquired Wendy's once before, and this fall proposed to buy it again by taking the chain private with the backing of a major franchisee. Wright is standing in his way.

It's a difficult moment for the burger chain. Wendy's lost its place as the second-largest burger chain by U.S. sales to Burger King earlier this year. It has reported seven straight quarters of same-store sales declines. Its shares have roughly halved in value since Peltz left as the company's chairman in 2024.

Restaurant chains are in a rough patch. Companies are fighting for customers and pumping out deals, while weathering increasing costs for beef and other necessities. The squeeze has triggered a string of takeover efforts and franchisee bankruptcies this year, including one of Wendy's largest operators.

At stake is the future of one of America's biggest burger brands, with 7,200 stores globally. The dust-up has left some Wendy's franchisees perplexed about the future, and not wanting to have to pick between a CEO they support and a franchisee they admire. Even Thomas's children, who still own and run restaurants in Ohio, have had questions.

For Peltz, Wendy's is one of his oldest holdings, and one of the few companies where he remains personally invested. Peltz served as board chairman, and his hedge fund Trian Fund Management held as many as three additional board seats.

The relationship is so personal Peltz serves Wendy's fare at family events. At his daughter Nicola's wedding to Brooklyn Beckham in Palm Beach, Fla., a Wendy's food truck served burgers, fries and Frosty desserts.

But his interest in the brand is also rooted in a financial calculation.

"Food companies tend to have brands that produce significant cash flow, even when they are neglected," Peltz said in a 2007 interview.

Wendy's stock roughly quadrupled from Trian's acquisition through 2024. Trian, Peltz and his associates had a more than 16% stake in Wendy's as of their latest filing, currently valued at around $267 million.

Since Peltz left as chairman, however, the stock has plunged.

In February, he said enough was enough. Peltz had previously explored takeovers of the company, and now Trian said it was examining strategic alternatives for Wendy's. "The company's common stock is currently undervalued," Trian said in a filing.

Wendy's had gone through three CEOs since 2024. In May, it turned to Wright who had done two prior stints as the company, the last ending in 2019.

After leaving Wendy's, Wright had turned around sandwich chain Potbelly's business. He had kept close tabs on the brand through the years, remaining in touch with franchisees and sampling Frosty desserts and Baconators when on the road. He kept binders of Thomas's original training material, boxes of Wendy's souvenirs and a version of the founder's signature white, button-down shirt and red tie at home.

When Wendy's called earlier this year about the CEO role, the 58-year-old father of three adult children consulted with his wife. Was she up for him taking on both a turnaround and a high-profile activist investor? he asked.

"I'm not blind to any of those circumstances and what the implications of those circumstances are," Wright said in an interview.

With his wife's blessing, Wright took the job and within weeks, started making executive changes. He was blunt with his team saying he'd had some subpar dining experiences at Wendy's and that the brand needed to improve its food and operations.

Wright's battle plan, called Dave's Way, a nod to the company's founder, wouldn't come cheap. He slashed the company's dividend in half in August and pulled financial guidance, saying Wendy's needed to invest to grow again. He promised thicker bacon, a creamier Frosty and bringing back whole-leaf lettuce from shredded leaves he viewed as subpar to attract more customers.

Meanwhile, Peltz was trying to move ahead with his own plan. And he found an ally in Greg Flynn, a star in the franchising world who does billions of dollars in business. Flynn had scooped up roughly 1,100 Pizza Hut and Wendy's restaurants through a bankruptcy auction in 2021.

San Francisco-based Flynn Group's holdings, which also includes hotels and real estate, was generating billions in annual sales, and had grown larger than many of the franchisers Flynn worked for.

Flynn has explored partnering with buyers of some of the brands he owns franchises in, including Pizza Hut when it was recently put up for sale, according to people familiar with the discussions. He'd grown increasingly confident in his ability to make brands run better.

"We've been able to get more out of those same operators than they were delivering for the last guys," Flynn, 62, said in an interview earlier this year.

Flynn, now with more than 300 Wendy's across three countries, wanted more from the brand. He'd been frustrated with the pace of action. Getting approval to update the brand's menu, color scheme and logo as part of his entry into Australia and New Zealand was slow, for instance, the people said.

Flynn and Peltz got to work lining up financing for their bid. They tapped private-credit firm Sixth Street, which Flynn knew from San Francisco and prior investments. BlueFive Capital, a Dubai-based investment firm with real estate and hospitality holdings, was also recruited.

In late October, a week before Wendy's reported quarterly earnings, Flynn and Peltz went live with their proposal: They offered to buy the company for $1.4 billion.

Wright wasn't totally surprised it had come to this. Wendy's had hired advisers to respond if Trian went forward with putting together a takeover plan.

The company's board took about a week before they rejected the offer and adopted a poison pill to block any potential hostile takeover.

Board chair Arthur Winkleblack said: "We believe in Bob."

During an industry conference in Las Vegas weeks later, Peltz's takeover proposal came up during a panel about challenging restaurant financing.

On the panel, Cristin O'Hara, a managing director for Bank of America, fielded questions about the deal. "If anyone can turn that around, it's him," she said, referring to Flynn. (Bank of America is working on Flynn and Trian's offer, though O'Hara isn't involved.)

Afterward, a representative for the trust representing the Wendy's founder's children rushed up to O'Hara to ask what the takeover bid meant for the chain. Even Wendy Thomas, whose childhood redheaded pigtails inspired the logo, had questions about the plans, he said.

O'Hara reassured him the situation wouldn't become hostile.

But the fight over who controls Wendy's isn't over. Advisors to the potential acquirers expect them to come up with a higher bid, though insist the takeover effort won't become hostile. Flynn has too much at stake as a top franchisee to get into a fight with one of his restaurant brands, they said.

Wendy's investors appear to be expecting a higher bid or for the turnaround to take root. Shares are up around 8% since the rejection.

Earlier this week, as Wright awaited the birth of a grandchild, he texted with Thomas. She owns restaurants in the Columbus, Ohio, area, and was about to open a new one. She asked Wright if it was OK to deviate from Wendy's rules on design. She wanted to include some nostalgic touches in the decor in tribute to her dad.

He agreed to her request and said he looked forward to personally visiting the new restaurant soon.

Write to Heather Haddon at heather.haddon@wsj.com

data.title: Zero To Sixty: Tesla Expands Cybercab To Dallas As Waymo Pauses Freeway Operations This Week
data.description:
Key points:
  • Tesla launched public Cybercab rides in Dallas, its second U.S. city after Austin, this week. 
  • Alphabet’s Waymo temporarily halted robotaxi operations on freeways across all U.S. markets after California’s Department of Motor Vehicles barred the company from state freeways. 
  • Lucid CEO said in a CNBC interview that the company does not expect the tax credit on EV purchases to be reinstated.

Tesla pushed further into autonomous vehicles this week with expanded Cybercab operations and new personal-use options, while rival robotaxi operator Waymo faced regulatory setbacks on freeways. Rivian’s dual-class share structure expired, reducing founder RJ Scaringe’s voting power, while Lucid Motors said the company is not awaiting a reinstatement of tax credits on EV purchases even as its deliveries continue to slide.

Tesla Rolls Out Cybercabs In Dallas, Invites Select Users To Make Purchase

Tesla launched public Cybercab rides in Dallas, its second U.S. city after Austin, this week. While Tesla offered robotaxi rides in Dallas before, the fleet only included Model Y vehicles. The Cybercab, in comparison, is the company’s dedicated two-seater robotaxi offering with no steering wheel or pedals.

The company also opened reservations to a limited group of invited customers near Austin for personal ownership of the vehicle at $29,990, paired with a $299 monthly autonomy subscription and strict rules against modifications or resale. Tesla intends to operate Cybercabs by itself in its robotaxi fleet while also selling it to fleet and individual customers in the long term.

Separately, Elon Musk appeared at the Dealbook Summit on Wednesday and said Tesla also plans a driverless Model Y variant without a steering wheel or pedals, aimed at groups of six or seven.

“It's going to make sense for us to make cars that can seat different amounts of people. We still need autonomous vehicles if you've got 4 or 6, or a whole family,” Musk said about the decision.

The moves come as Tesla seeks to pivot into artificial intelligence and robotics, and away from just consumer cars. The company is also reportedly planning a €3 billion ($3.3 billion) investment in its German plant as it seeks to expand Cybercab production outside the U.S. According to a report from Reuters on Monday, Tesla plans to construct an additional production facility at its German gigafactory with the aim of producing a million units of its Cybercab robotaxis there.

Waymo Pauses Freeway Robotaxi Service After California Ban

Tesla’s robotaxi rival, Alphabet’s Waymo, meanwhile, temporarily halted robotaxi operations on freeways across all U.S. markets after California’s Department of Motor Vehicles barred the company from state freeways, citing an “imminent hazard” from multiple incidents in which vehicles entered active construction zones.

According to a report from Reuters, Waymo subsequently said it filed two safety recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) for its automated driving system “to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control.”

Rivian's Dual-Class Share Structure Expires

Rivian’s dual-class share structure ended this week. On November 15, the five-year anniversary of its IPO closing, all remaining Class B shares, which carried 10 votes each, automatically converted one-for-one into ordinary Class A shares.

The conversion reduced founder and CEO RJ Scaringe’s voting power to roughly 0.5%, aligning it with his economic ownership.

Lucid CEO Says Not Counting On Democrats To Restore EV Tax Credits

CEO of Lucid Motors, which is facing slumping deliveries, said in a CNBC interview this week that the company is not expecting the tax credit on EV purchases to be reinstated. The federal incentive was rescinded last year by President Trump and has hit the sales of EV makers, including Lucid. Talking about whether the company expects its reinstatement following Democrats taking control of Congress following the midterm elections, Lucid CEO Silvio Napoli said the company will take “any positive. ”

“You know, they say, ‘Plan for the worst and … hope for the best.’ That’s all we can say,” Napoli said.

How Did Retail Traders React?

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around TSLA was ‘neutral’ at the time of writing, while sentiment around LCID, RIVN and GOOGL was more ‘bearish.’

All four stocks closed in the red this week, amid a larger tech sell-off, with LCID and RIVN leading the pack by clocking a 15% loss. TSLA dropped 11% while GOOGL dropped 10%.

data.title: How Mercedes-Benz Nearly Became Collateral Damage in a Chinese Car Ban — WSJ
data.description:
By Ryan Felton, Stephen Wilmot and Gavin Bade

For Mercedes-Benz, the outcome would be catastrophic.

If Congress passed legislation banning Chinese cars from the U.S., the German automaker feared becoming collateral damage — forced out of the American market because Chinese entities hold a nearly 20% stake in the company.

It would mean that Mercedes, whose vehicles have been on American roads since the 19th century and which operates factories in Alabama and South Carolina, would lose access to one of its most important global markets.

For months, lawmakers said that the idea of the U.S. losing a familiar auto brand that has invested heavily in American production would be unfathomable. But as pressure mounted to pass the bill before a lame-duck session of Congress ends in the coming weeks, Mercedes was left without clear answers about its future.

Now, survival in the U.S. looks far more likely for Mercedes.

Lawmakers are nearing a deal to keep the automaker in the American market if the anti-Chinese car bill passes, so long as Mercedes reduces its Chinese ownership stake in the coming years or is granted a waiver from the U.S. Commerce Department, according to people familiar with the matter.

The bills, which include versions working through the House and Senate, target companies with more than 15% ownership by Chinese entities from operating in the U.S. The state-owned Chinese automaker BAIC Group and Li Shufu, chairman of China's Geely Holding Group, together own nearly 20% of Mercedes.

New provisions in the bill under consideration keep the 15% threshold intact, but could allow for Mercedes to remain in the U.S., pending a review by the Commerce Department, the people said. Bloomberg earlier reported on details of the arrangement.

Mercedes supports the provision, some of the people said, pending final details. "We continue to meet with all stakeholders who have a shared interest in ensuring this important legislation becomes law in this Congress," Mercedes said in a statement.

The United Auto Workers union, which has endorsed legislation banning Chinese cars, originally stood in the way of a deal to allow Mercedes to remain until intense negotiations took place Thursday. The union opposed a specific carve-out for Mercedes but has agreed to the latest terms, some of the people said. Mercedes' U.S. factories aren't unionized.

A UAW spokesman declined to comment.

Chinese cars are currently banned from the U.S. because of restrictions on connected hardware and software, as well as onerous tariffs. The bills would attempt to codify those rules into law.

Lawmakers and the auto industry as a whole have warned that allowing Chinese cars into the U.S. would decimate jobs and profits for existing auto manufacturers, as has happened in other markets around the world. They argue that China's auto industry has been heavily subsidized by the country's government and would present unfair competition to established players. Lawmakers also fear that Chinese cars could spy on U.S. citizens and sensitive facilities.

While auto industry officials support the bills, they have been stymied for months as automakers haggle over specifics, often trying to undercut rivals or protect their own interests. They quibbled over parts with Chinese content, such as air bags and battery components. Others raised concerns about whether the legislation goes far enough; it targets internet-connected cars, but some lawmakers wanted Chinese ownership alone to be grounds for a ban.

Additional details are still being discussed and the bill continues to work through Congress. Lawmakers have been racing to finish the bill soon to avoid a restart next year.

"We're working on this nonstop," said Rep. Debbie Dingell (D., Mich.). "It is a top priority. China is stealing our intellectual property now. This is a national security issue."

But Mercedes proved to be an unexpected wrinkle in an effort that has otherwise seen broad support from both parties.

A ban from Washington would be unthinkable for Mercedes-Benz. The U.S. accounted for a quarter of its revenue in the first three quarters of 2026, and its share has been rising as its business in China has buckled under pressure from local competitors and a weak market. Automakers across the world are seeking to increase their U.S. market share as profits from the once-lucrative Chinese market evaporate.

Mercedes also has a large manufacturing footprint in the U.S. that would make little sense if it didn't have a major local market to serve. Its flagship plant in Alabama turns out high-end luxury SUVs, including big-engined GLE and GLS models.

Including its headquarters in Atlanta and a smaller van-assembly plant in Charleston, S.C., the company has roughly 10,000 employees in the U.S.

In a statement, Mercedes said it complies with applicable local laws, and underlined planned investments of almost $8 billion in the U.S. by 2030.

This week, the House Select Committee on China sent a letter to Mercedes-Benz demanding exhaustive details of its links to Chinese companies, with a deadline of Dec. 1.

The committee demanded anything relating to Mercedes's shareholders as well as its Chinese suppliers. It asked for a model-by-model breakdown of Chinese parts in its cars sold in the U.S., and details of any concerns expressed "formally or informally" about its links to China by board directors or company officers in the past decade.

Efforts to ban Chinese cars in the U.S. have already affected other automakers. Volvo, which is majority-owned by Geely, received a carve-out after a lengthy process to show the Commerce Department how it would protect the U.S. national interest. But the Polestar electric-vehicle brand, also owned by Geely, was banned.

data.title: India's IndusInd Bank ends ex-CEO Kathpalia's employment, seeks to recover pay
data.description:
IndusInd Bank said on Friday it has terminated former top boss Sumant Kathpalia's employment with the bank and is seeking to recover pay spanning his entire tenure, following a disciplinary inquiry.

Kathpalia resigned in April 2025 after IndusInd Bank disclosed incorrect accounting on derivative trades that prompted a $230 million hit to its accounts, throwing the private-sector lender into a crisis that hit its shares and drew regulatory scrutiny.

The bank told Kathpalia he would remain in employment and then initiated disciplinary proceedings against him. In June 2025 he was suspended, pending completion of the proceedings.

Based on the findings of an inquiry report this week, the bank's board decided to terminate Kathpalia's employment and invoke applicable malus and clawback provisions with effect from the date of his initial appointment as CEO in March 2020.

IndusInd did not disclose details of the inquiry's findings. Reuters could not reach Kathpalia for comment.

Reuters had reported in November 2025 that the lender had begun a process to claw back salary and bonuses from Kathpalia and former deputy CEO Arun Khurana, after an internal review flagged misconduct and misreporting.

Indian banking regulations have allowed clawback provisions in employee contracts since 2019 to deter misconduct, but such efforts have been rare.

IndusInd's loans and deposits returned to double-digit growth in the second quarter of the current fiscal year, the first time since the accounting discrepancies emerged. Its shares are up 16% this year after dropping 10% in 2025.
